Mining · Zimbabwe

Know what is changing on and around your mining location

Zimbabwe’s Mines and Minerals Act keeps prospecting and mining set distances away from homesteads, cultivated land, roads, railways, pipelines and power lines. We give your land, community and environment teams one dated, reviewed record of the structures, pits, spoil, cleared ground and tracks inside and around your location, whether it is platinum-group metal ground on the Great Dyke, a lithium claim or a gold working, so every conversation starts from the same facts.

Send us your location boundary See sample outputs

The problem, in your words

Ground that changes between visits

“New pits keep opening on and around our claims.”

Pits, spoil and water-filled excavations appear between visits, on the location itself or along its edge. A dated map of where and when is the start of every conversation about them.

“Homes are going up close to our boundary.”

Ground within 450 m of a principal homestead is not open to prospecting without the owner’s written consent (s.31). When a structure first appears in the imagery can matter as much as where it stands.

“We have to show the title is being worked.”

On 10 June 2025 Cabinet said that “use it/lose it” would be strengthened (Post-Cabinet briefing). Dated imagery of the ground over the years shows what was worked, cleared or built, and when.

“The plant expansion needs a baseline.”

Mining is a First Schedule project that needs an EMA certificate before it is implemented, and where people live on a new footprint, lenders ask for a record of what stood there on the cut-off date.

Who this is for

  • Mine land and tenure managers
  • Community-relations and social-performance teams
  • Environment and EMA compliance officers
  • Exploration and claims teams
  • Mine surveyors and GIS teams, as users
  • ESIA and RAP consultants
  • Lenders’ environmental and social advisers

The distances in the Act

What the Mines and Minerals Act keeps mining away from

The Mines and Minerals Act [Chapter 21:05] closes some ground to prospecting without consent (s.31) and keeps mining itself away from infrastructure (s.34) (Mines and Minerals Act). Each distance is a band we can report, around your boundary or around the working areas you define.

Near Distance Rule
A principal homestead, built or registered as an intended site 450 m Not open to prospecting without the owner’s, or on communal land the occupier’s, written consent (s.31)
Farm-worker housing, dip tanks, and buildings and permanent improvements above a value threshold 90 m The same (s.31)
Land under cultivation On it or within 15 m The same (s.31)
Other farm buildings 9 m The same, unless compensated (s.31)
The middle of a road 15 m No mining (s.34)
A railway track 45 m No mining, including mining buildings (s.34)
A pipeline 5 m, or 25 m for asbestos pipelines over 30 cm No prospecting or mining without the owner’s consent (s.34(7))
A power line 10, 25 or 40 m from the centre line, by voltage No prospecting or mining (s.34(8))

Section 31 also closes other mining locations, town limits plus a 50 m belt, aerodromes, State rifle ranges, any railway reserve, cemeteries, holdings of 100 ha or less without consent, and “Communal Land occupied as a village without the written consent of the rural district council”. Around pipelines the 2026 Pipelines Act adds a wider rule: no mining or blasting within 125 m of either side of the centre (Act No. 5 of 2025). More on pipeline reserves and power-line wayleaves in Zimbabwe.

Checked 27 September 2026

Read from ZimLII’s consolidated text of the Act. Parliament is considering a new Mines and Minerals Bill (H.B. 1, 2025), which was still before the National Assembly on 22 September 2026 (Veritas). This is a summary, not legal advice.

Pits, spoil and cleared ground

A dated map of the ground disturbance on and around your location

New pits, spoil heaps, water-filled excavations, cleared ground and new tracks inside your location and in a ring around it are mapped from dated imagery, with new sites flagged between surveys and confirmed by a reviewer. Each record carries its coordinates, its distance to your boundary and to the working areas you define, and the imagery date on which it first appears. In the rainy season, radar comparisons show larger ground changes even under cloud, and flagged areas are followed up with optical imagery or your own drone flights.

What we map is the ground. We never identify, count or follow people, and underground workings and covered shafts are not visible from above. Artisanal mining is one of the sectors reserved exclusively for Zimbabweans (S.I. 215 of 2025); whether a mapped pit is on your ground, and who holds rights to it, is for your tenure team and the authorities. A flagged site is an indication for your teams to check, not proof of anything.

What you receive

  • Pits, spoil, water-filled excavations and cleared ground, located and dated
  • New tracks and access routes into the location
  • New and removed structures at the boundary and in a ring around it
  • Change between dated surveys, confirmed by a reviewer
  • A PDF report and GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers

Plants, dumps and new footprints

Record the footprint before it changes

Mineral prospecting and mining are First Schedule projects under the Environmental Management Act and need an EMA certificate before they are implemented (s.97). Beneficiation policy is adding plant: Cabinet announced on 10 June 2025 that lithium sulphate value-addition facilities are being established and that “with effect from January 2027 the export of lithium concentrate will no longer be allowed”, and linked new chrome titles above 100 ha to furnace capacity (Post-Cabinet briefing).

When a plant, pit, dump or tailings facility is planned, we produce a dated record of the structures in the footprint, with reviewer categories such as main building, outbuilding, livestock enclosure or under construction, and on request estimated households with the assumptions stated. It supports the census, asset inventory and cut-off-date records; categories describe what the imagery shows, not use, ownership or value. For blast radii and tailings zones, your engineers supply the zones and we list the structures inside them.

Baselines for new ground

  • Structures in the footprint on the cut-off date
  • Structures inside the blast and tailings zones you define
  • A land-use and land-cover baseline before disturbance
  • Rehabilitation and revegetation trends afterwards

Imagery history

What the ground looked like before the question was asked

Boundary disagreements, tenure reviews and “use it/lose it” enforcement all turn on what was on the ground, and when. From archived satellite imagery and open datasets we document a location, a claim or a disputed strip year by year: what was built, cleared, excavated or worked, with each scene named and dated. We work from the boundaries you give us; confirming a boundary on the ground, or placing beacons, is a registered land surveyor’s work.

Imagery history and land due diligence

Already flying drones?

We analyse your own imagery

CAAZ’s 2025 annual report records 54 drones over 2 kg registered that year. If your team or a contractor already flies the location, the flying is done; turning each set of orthophotos into a list of what is new, where and how close it is to your boundary is the part we add. Send the orthophotos or GeoTIFFs and we run the excavation, structure and change analysis on them, with a person reviewing every result and dated satellite scenes between flights.

New drone surveys, where you want them, are subject to the CAAZ approvals and security clearances each operation requires, including written approvals from landowners and local authorities and the owner’s permission to fly within 30 m of any structure. Afridrone is working towards the approvals Zimbabwe requires.

Personal data on a mine

A register of structures linked to occupants is personal information under the Cyber and Data Protection Act. POTRAZ is the Data Protection Authority, and Veritas reports POTRAZ inspections from 1 September 2026, with “mining enterprises” fifth of the nine categories listed (Veritas). Settle the controller and processor roles, and whether a data controller licence is needed, before a register is built.

How it works

From boundary file to reviewed record

  1. Scope

    You send the location, claim or lease boundaries, the working areas and the distances to report, and say what the record is for: boundary change, excavation, an expansion or a tenure question. It all goes into a written proposal.

  2. Map from imagery

    Dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or your own orthophotos give the first record of structures, pits and cleared ground inside and around the location.

  3. Compare between dates

    Later surveys, on a schedule you agree, flag what is new or gone, with radar in the rainy season and your own flights where you have them.

  4. Review and deliver

    A person checks every result before the report and GIS layers go to the contacts you name.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Map pits, spoil, cleared ground, tracks and structures visible from the air
  • Measure each record to your boundary and working areas, at the distances you set
  • Flag change between dated surveys, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Document the imagery history of a location or claim

What we don’t do

  • Identify, count or follow people, or say who is digging
  • See underground workings or covered shafts
  • Verify title, place beacons or carry out land surveys
  • Decide whether a structure or a pit is lawful

Frequently asked questions

What is the 450 metre homestead rule?

Under section 31 of the Mines and Minerals Act, ground within 450 m of a principal homestead, built or registered as an intended site, is not open to prospecting without the written consent of the owner or, on communal land, the occupier. Shorter distances protect farm-worker housing, dip tanks and valuable permanent improvements (90 m), land under cultivation (15 m) and other farm buildings (9 m). We map the structures and cultivated ground around your location, with the imagery date on which each first appears.

How close can mining come to a road, railway, pipeline or power line?

Section 34 bars mining within 15 m of the middle of a road and within 45 m of a railway track, including mining buildings; within 5 m of most pipelines, or 25 m of large asbestos pipelines, without the owner’s consent; and within 10, 25 or 40 m of the centre line of a power line, depending on voltage. Since 16 February 2026 the Pipelines Act also forbids mining and blasting within 125 m of either side of a pipeline’s centre.

Can you show digging on our claim that we did not authorise?

We show the ground: new pits, spoil heaps, water-filled excavations, cleared ground and tracks, each located and dated, flagged between surveys and confirmed by a reviewer. We never identify, count or follow people, and underground workings and covered shafts are not visible from above. Who is working the ground, and under what title, is for your tenure team and the authorities.

Can you confirm our location boundary?

No. We work from the boundary you give us and do not verify title or tenure. Boundary and beacon surveys are reserved to practising land surveyors (Land Survey Act s.16). What we can add is the imagery history of the ground along a disputed boundary.

Can your baseline replace our resettlement census?

No. A dated record of the structures in an expansion footprint supports your census, asset inventory and valuation, and the cut-off-date records lenders ask for. It does not replace them. The Constitution requires a court order, made after considering all the relevant circumstances, before anyone is evicted from their home or has it demolished (s.74), and our records are designed to support fair, transparent processes.

Is the Mines and Minerals Act about to change?

Parliament is considering a new Mines and Minerals Bill (H.B. 1, 2025). As at 22 September 2026 it was still before the National Assembly, which was considering the Parliamentary Legal Committee’s adverse report on it. The distances on this page are those of the Act in force.

Send us your location boundary

Shapefile, GeoPackage, KML or GeoJSON of the location, claims or lease, with any working areas, dumps or plant sites, and the distances you want reported. Tell us what imagery you already fly. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
